notes.short: One prophet of the LORD against Baal's 450
notes.about: Elijah stands alone on Carmel, calling himself “the only remaining prophet of the LORD,” against Baal's 450. They shout, leap and cut themselves from morning to evening, and no one answers. Many also set his one short, calm prayer against their cries. Then the fire of the LORD falls.

sides.label: One prophet, one short prayer
sides.words: I am the only remaining prophet of the LORD

sides.label: Many, crying out all day unanswered
sides.words: they kept on raving until the time of the evening sacrifice

notes.evidence: Matthew Henry: Baal's cause had 450 men, God's but one; Elijah's short, calm prayer was far from their frenzy. George Rawlinson (Barnes' Notes): Elijah sets his lone stand against the crowd. Alfred Barry (Ellicott's Commentary): their wild cry stands against Elijah's simple prayer. Alexander Maclaren: alone, Elijah towers above the crowd; his calm prayer is in sharp contrast with their cries.
notes.limit: He was not the only one left who was faithful: Obadiah had hidden a hundred prophets of the LORD, and God kept seven thousand in Israel who had not bowed to Baal.

cites.quote: The managers of Baal's cause were 450 men, fat and well fed ... The manager of God's cause was but one man, lately a poor exile, hardly kept from starving ... His prayer was not long, for he used no vain repetitions ... but it was very grave and composed, and showed his mind to be calm and sedate, and far from the heats and disorders that Baal's prophets were in

The others ... had been forced to fly and hide themselves in dens and caves of the earth; their voices were silenced; they had not ventured to come to Carmel. Elijah contrasts his solitary appearance on the side of Yahweh at the great gathering with the crowd of those opposed to him.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: This repeated cry ... uttered probably first in measured chant, afterwards in a wild excited cry ... stands in an instructive contrast ... with the simple, earnest solemnity of the prayer of Elijah.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

cites.quote: Then Elijah takes the command, and, though utterly alone, towers above the crowd in the courage of his undaunted confidence in his message ... The tranquil though earnest prayer of the prophet is in sharpest contrast with the meaningless bellowings to Baal.

notes.short: Elijah's taunt: “Shout louder, for he is a god!”
notes.about: Elijah taunts the prophets of Baal: shout louder, for he is a god, perhaps lost in thought, busy, travelling or asleep. He means the opposite. Baal does not answer because he is no god, and the taunt drives them on until all can see that no one answered (verse 29).

figure.name: Irony
figure.words: Shout louder, for he is a god!
figure.means: that Baal is no god at all, since he cannot hear or answer however loud they cry

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the words under Irony as sarcasm of the severest kind. Adam Clarke calls them a strong irony, and Robert Jamieson (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) says Elijah exposed their folly with the severest irony. George Rawlinson (Barnes' Notes) says the irony spurred the priests on, so that failure would prove Baal no God. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) hears derision: a god in their opinion only.

cites.at: Eironeia, or Irony: Human Irony, p. 813
cites.quote: The words of Elijah to the prophets of Baal were sarcasm of the severest kind.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: he is the supreme God, you worship him as such, he must needs be such, and no doubt jealous of his own honor and the credit of his votaries! A strong irony.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: No response was heard. No fire descended. Elijah exposed their folly and imposture with the severest irony
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The object of Elijah's irony was two-fold; (1) to stimulate the priests to greater exertions, and so to make their failure more complete, and (2) to suggest to the people that such failure would prove absolutely that Baal was no God.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: As no answer had been received before noon, Elijah cried out to them in derision ... for he is God (sc., according to your opinion) ... The ridicule lies more especially in the ... (for he is a god), when contrasted with the enumeration of the different possibilities which may have occasioned their obtaining no answer

notes.short: Micaiah echoes the false prophets in mockery
notes.about: Micaiah answers with the same promise the king's prophets gave (verse 12), but he means the opposite, and Ahab hears it: he makes him swear to tell only the truth (verse 16). Then Micaiah tells what he saw, Israel scattered on the hills like sheep without a shepherd.

figure.name: Irony
figure.means: that Ahab will not triumph: Micaiah mocks the promise of the king's false prophets

original.note: In Hebrew Micaiah's answer repeats the prophets' words in verse 12, with the same verbs for “go up” and “prosper”; the BSB says “triumph” here.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the answer under Irony, showing up the false prophecies of Ahab's own prophets. Adam Clarke calls it a strong irony. George Rawlinson (Barnes' Notes) and Robert Jamieson (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) say Micaiah used the prophets' words in a mocking, ironical tone, and Matthew Henry that he spoke as they had, but ironically.

cites.at: Eironeia, or Irony: Human Irony, p. 813
cites.quote: The words of the prophet Micaiah to Ahab and Jehoshaphat: “Go, and prosper”; to show by Irony the false prophecies of Ahab’s own prophets.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: This was a strong irony; as if he had said, All your prophets have predicted success; you wish me to speak as they speak ... spoken by Micaiah in such a tone and manner as at once showed to Ahab that he did not believe them
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Micaiah speaks the exact words of the 400 in so mocking and ironical a tone, that the king cannot mistake his meaning, or regard his answer as serious.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: the prophet gave precisely the same answer as the previous oracles that had been consulted; but it must have been given in a sarcastic tone and in ironical mockery of their way of speaking.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: He spoke as the rest of the prophets had spoken, but ironically: Go, and prosper ... with such an air and pronunciation as plainly showed he spoke it by way of derision
